closest_prior.how_this_differs: Wildgaard et al. catalogue 108 author-level indicators including a category for 'impact over time', so a fixed-age-window aggregate is almost certainly inside that taxonomy. The project differs only in evaluating indicator choice against a pre-registered, co-author-split future-citation outcome on one field (IR) across two citation indexes. That is a different question from 'is this indicator well-behaved', and it is the project's actual contribution.

Clermont et al. test citation-window length at the publication/chair level in business, biology and medicine, and conclude short windows are already informative for ranking order. The project asks the same question at the author level in computer science. If fixed-age windows do not move the ranking, this paper predicted it and the project's result becomes a confirmation, not a discovery.

Waltman & Schreiber give the correct percentile computation including tie handling. The project does not invent a percentile rule; it imports this one and measures whether percentiles beat the project's A1 share metric on the co-author-split future-citation outcome, which that paper does not test.

This already proposes an author- and age-normalised logarithmic index, so 'correct author metrics for age' is solved in that strand. The project's angle is measurement of whether a correction works on its own benchmark, with a false fix (the deflator) already documented.

If the project ever runs PageRank, this paper is the direct benchmark and it reports PageRank does not clearly outperform simple counts. The project should not re-derive that; it should cite it and, if it runs PageRank at all, run it as a replication with the shared outcome.

novelty: Not novel as an indicator. Both remaining candidate metrics are named, published and reviewed: fixed-age/citation-window normalisation (Wildgaard 2014; Clermont 2020; Gyorffy 2026; the 2015 age-normalised log index) and percentile scores (Waltman & Schreiber 2013; Bornmann 2013 PR6/PR8). Nothing found does the project's specific comparison: same data, same future-citation outcome, same co-author-split denominator, evaluating a family of author metrics against each other with pre-registered hypotheses. The genuine contribution is the evaluation design plus one negative result already banked (the deflator fails to fix age bias while costing accuracy). Concretely: do not frame either metric as an invention. Frame the project as an evaluation, adopt the published definitions verbatim (percentile ties from Waltman & Schreiber; fractional counting from Waltman & van Eck 2015), and pre-register a hypothesis that the published result could falsify, e.g. that a fixed-age window does not reduce age bias in IR, which follows from Clermont 2020. A surprise is then informative and its absence is a confirmation rather than a null result.
